Ask or Delegate? How the World Uses AI Differently

Model report 3 — Diversity in a Globalized World

Author

Popescu (example report)

Published

September 9, 2026

Show Code 
library(sf)
library(ggplot2)

countries <- readRDS("data/ai/preprocessed_data/countries.rds")

The question

A trade shock arrives in a place whether anyone wants it or not. A factory closes; nobody in the town chose that. Most of what we study in this course works that way — it happens to people.

AI is different. It arrives as a website. Anyone with a connection can open it, and every person who does decides what to ask it for. So the interesting question is not only where AI reaches, but what people decide to do with it once it gets there.

Our question: does AI get used the same way everywhere?

Why we thought it might not

The obvious guess is that it does. Unlike a factory or a port, this technology is identical everywhere. The same model, the same interface, the same price.

But a tool is not only its design. A hammer in a workshop and a hammer in a museum are the same object doing different things. If AI lands in a country where most users are students, it will be used for one thing. If it lands where most users are professionals, another.

So we expected the purposes to differ even though the tool does not.

What we are working with

Anthropic, which makes the AI assistant Claude, classified millions of real conversations and published country-level totals: what share was work, what share was studying, and whether people handed over a whole task or worked alongside the model.

We have 121 countries for May 2026. Each row is one country.

Show Code 
countries |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  subset(iso3 %in% c("MEX","USA","TUN","NOR"),
         select = c(country, adoption_rate, used_for_study, automation_style))
                     country adoption_rate used_for_study automation_style
17  United States of America         20.16           8.94            49.59
38                   Tunisia          0.27          51.52            49.79
89                    Norway          0.35          26.38            41.26
110                   Mexico          1.32          21.08            50.36

Two columns matter most here.

used_for_study is the share of conversations that are coursework. automation_style is the share where someone handed over an entire task rather than working through it together — asking for the finished thing instead of asking for help.

One warning before we start, and we return to it at the end. This describes people who use Claude, not people in general. Look at adoption_rate: the United States is around 20, Tunisia around 0.3. Both numbers are real, but they describe very different slices of a population.

Map 1 — Where AI is used for studying

Show Code 
ggplot(countries) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = used_for_study), color = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "rocket", direction = -1, na.value = "grey93",
                       name = "% of use") +
  labs(title = "Share of AI use that is coursework, May 2026") +
  coord_sf(crs = "+proj=robin") +
  theme_void()

The pattern is not subtle. Across North Africa, the Andes, much of sub-Saharan Africa and Indonesia, a large share of everything people ask AI for is schoolwork. In North America and Western Europe it is a small share.

Tunisia is the extreme: more than half of all use is coursework. In the United States it is under one in ten. Mexico sits at about 21%.

The grey countries have no data. Claude is not used everywhere, and that absence is worth noticing too.

Map 2 — Where people hand over the whole task

The second map asks something different: not what for, but how.

Show Code 
ggplot(countries) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = automation_style), color = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "mako", direction = -1, na.value = "grey93",
                       name = "% of use") +
  labs(title = "Share of use where the whole task is handed over") +
  coord_sf(crs = "+proj=robin") +
  theme_void()

Compare it with Map 1. The dark areas are largely the same places. Where AI is used most for studying, it is also used most for delegating.

Map 3 — How widely AI has spread

Show Code 
ggplot(countries) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = adoption_rate), color = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "viridis", direction = -1, trans = "sqrt",
                       na.value = "grey93", name = "Adoption") +
  labs(title = "How much each country uses AI, relative to its size") +
  coord_sf(crs = "+proj=robin") +
  theme_void()

This is nearly the negative of the first two. The countries that delegate most and study most are the countries where AI has spread least.

Three maps, and a pattern that repeats. The next step is to put two of them together.

Simple graph — Studying and delegating

Each dot is a country. Going right means more of its AI use is coursework. Going up means more of it is handing over a whole task.

Show Code 
ggplot(countries, aes(x = used_for_study, y = automation_style)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 2, color = "#b44527") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "#0f6f96") +
  labs(title = "Countries that use AI to study also use it to delegate",
       x = "% of AI use that is coursework",
       y = "% of use where the whole task is handed over") +
  theme_minimal()

The line slopes upward clearly. This is the uncomfortable part of the finding, and it is worth stating carefully.

It would be reassuring if students used AI mainly to have things explained to them. In the countries where AI use is most concentrated in coursework, that is not what the pattern suggests. Those are the same countries where people most often ask for the finished answer rather than for help getting to it.

Complex graph — Does this change as AI spreads?

If delegation were simply a stage — what people do when a tool is new, before they learn to work with it — then countries where AI is more established should delegate less. We can check that by splitting the countries into four groups by how widely AI has spread.

Show Code 
d <- st_drop_geometry(countries)
d <- d[!is.na(d$used_for_study) & d$continent != "Seven seas (open ocean)", ]
d$spread <- cut(d$adoption_rate,
                breaks = quantile(d$adoption_rate, c(0, .25, .5, .75, 1)),
                labels = c("AI least widespread", "", " ", "AI most widespread"),
                include.lowest = TRUE)

ggplot(d, aes(x = used_for_study, y = automation_style)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = continent), alpha = 0.75, size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "grey30", linewidth = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ spread, nrow = 1) +
  labs(title = "The same relationship, from least to most widespread AI use",
       subtitle = "Countries move down and left as AI becomes more established",
       x = "% of AI use that is coursework",
       y = "% of use where the whole task is handed over",
       color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

Read the panels left to right. The cloud of countries slides down and to the left. Where AI is least widespread, countries sit high and right: heavy coursework use, heavy delegation. Where it is most widespread, they sit low and left.

The extremes make it concrete. Zimbabwe, Mongolia, Uganda and Rwanda delegate most — all with almost no AI adoption. Norway, Denmark and Belgium delegate least.

What we take from this

AI does not arrive the same way everywhere. The tool is identical; what it is used for is not. That is a fact about societies, not about technology, and it is the main thing this data shows.

Where AI is newest, it is used to study and to delegate. Those two go together strongly, and both are concentrated in countries where adoption is lowest.

Where AI is most established, people work with it rather than hand things to it. The shift from delegating to collaborating looks like something that happens as a society gains experience with a tool.

But we cannot tell whether that is learning or something else. Countries where AI is widespread are also richer, older, and have more people already in professional work. Any of those could produce the same pattern. We are looking at a snapshot of 121 countries at one moment, not at any country changing over time.

What the maps add: the scatter shows that studying and delegating go together. Only the maps show where — and seeing the same regions darken on Map 1 and Map 2, then lighten on Map 3, is what suggested the sequence in the first place.

What this report does not show

We are looking at Claude users, not populations. This is the most important limitation and it affects every sentence above. In Tunisia, roughly 0.3% of what adoption would look like at US levels is present — so “half of Tunisian use is coursework” describes a small, self-selected group, almost certainly younger, more urban and better connected than Tunisians in general. When we write “in country X, people use AI for…”, we always mean the people in country X who use Claude.

One company, one month. Claude is one AI assistant among several, and this is May 2026 alone. Users of other tools may behave differently.

No causation. We have shown that studying and delegating occur together, not that either causes the other, and not that countries change as adoption grows. We compared different countries at one moment, which is not the same as watching one country over time.

“Delegating” is a classification, not a judgement. Handing over a whole task is sometimes exactly the right thing to do. We should not read the map as showing where people are using AI badly.

How we used AI

What we did AI? What we asked How we checked
Fixing missing countries Yes Why France and Norway were blank on our map Found the country-code column was -99; checked against the data
Choosing a map projection Yes How to avoid Greenland dominating Compared three projections and chose Robinson
Deciding the question No — —
Writing the interpretation No — —

One prompt we used:

“I have an sf object called countries with a variable adoption_rate that is very skewed. My map is almost entirely one colour. What are my options and what does each one do to the reader’s impression?”

What we changed afterwards. It suggested three fixes and we chose the square root scale. But its last point was the useful one: any transformation changes what the reader sees, so we should say which one we used. That is why trans = "sqrt" is visible in the code above rather than hidden.
